research_thread.scientific_problem: Determining the optimal sintering temperature to maximize the synergy between mechanical properties, high-temperature oxidation resistance, and corrosion resistance in MgAlTiVFeCo lightweight high-entropy alloys.
research_thread.sample_lineage: Ball-milled powder (BCC solid solution) -> Spark Plasma Sintered bulk (BCC + secondary phases)
research_thread.intervention: Varying SPS sintering temperature from 850 °C to 1000 °C
research_thread.conditions: SPS at 1000 °C; Oxidation at 900 °C in air; Corrosion in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution
research_thread.structure: BCC primary phase with precipitation of secondary phases; dense microstructure at 1000 °C
research_thread.outcome: 1000 °C sample (LW1000) achieved 96.7% densification, 1235.5 HV hardness, lowest oxidation rate constants, and best corrosion resistance (most positive E_corr, lowest i_corr).
research_thread.mechanism: Diffusion-controlled oxidation (parabolic law) and passive film formation (Al/Fe spinels) enhanced by uniform distribution of barrier phases and increased relative density.
research_thread.hypothesis_value: High-temperature sintering (1000 °C) optimizes the trade-off between densification and secondary phase distribution, creating a microstructure that simultaneously acts as a diffusion barrier for oxidation and a support for a stable passive film for corrosion resistance.
alternative_explanations: Oxidation resistance might be driven solely by grain boundary density rather than specific phase distribution.
Corrosion improvement might be due to surface segregation of Mg rather than bulk phase distribution.
Hardness might be due to solid solution strengthening rather than secondary phase precipitation.
boundaries: Upper limit: 1000 °C (optimal; higher temperatures restricted by Mg volatility/reactivity)
missing_information: Chemical identity and morphology of the 'barrier phases' in the bulk microstructure.
Detailed grain size evolution across the 850-1000 °C range.
Specific composition of the passive film at the surface versus the bulk secondary phases.

evidence_spans: In this study, a MgAlTiVFeCo lightweight high-entropy alloy (LW-HEA) was fabricated via mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS) to investigate the effects of sintering temperature on its phase structure, microstructure, densification, microhardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance, and corrosion resistance.
The results indicate that the ball-milled MgAlTiVFeCo LW-HEA formed a simple solid solution phase with a BCC structure.
After spark plasma sintering, the phase structure of the alloy changed, maintaining the BCC phase as the primary phase while accompanying the precipitation of secondary phases.
When the sintering temperature reached 1000 °C, the alloy achieved a densification of 96.7% and a microhardness of 1235.5 HV.

The oxidation kinetics of MgAlTiVFeCo high-entropy alloys sintered at different temperatures at 900 °C follow a parabolic law, which is diffusion-controlled and can be divided into two stages: rapid growth and slow stabilization.

At a sintering temperature of 1000 °C, the fitted oxidation rate constants, k p1 (0–25 h) and k p2 (25–60 h), are 3.76 × 10 −2 mg 2 ·cm −4 ·s −1 and 1.10 × 10 −1 mg 2 ·cm −4 ·s −1 , respectively, outperforming those of alloys sintered at other temperatures.
In a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution, the corrosion resistance of the alloy improves with increasing sintering temperature.

Compared to alloys sintered at medium-to-low temperatures (850–950 °C), the alloy sintered at a high temperature (1000 °C) exhibits a more positive corrosion potential (−0.438 V) and a lower corrosion current density (1.07 × 10 −6 A·cm −2 ), indicating excellent corrosion resistance.
It is evident that 1000 °C is the optimal sintering temperature, and the MgAlTiVFeCo LW-HEA demonstrates superior comprehensive properties.

The covering and cooling effects of ethanol further slowed the reaction between fresh powder surfaces and residual oxygen; a high ball-to-powder ratio (10:1) was adopted to enhance alloying efficiency, shorten the total time required to achieve sufficient alloying, and thereby indirectly reduce the exposure time of the powder in its active state to a potentially oxidizing environment

Given the extremely high chemical reactivity of magnesium, multiple strategies were employed synergistically throughout the milling process to control its oxidation tendency; for example, MgAl pre-alloyed powder was used instead of pure magnesium powder to reduce the surface reactivity of magnesium via pre-alloying; after loading the powders, anhydrous ethanol was added to the milling jar for wet milling.

For the nanocrystalline powder obtained by high-energy ball milling in this system, when the SPS temperature was lower than 800 °C, the sintering driving force was insufficient, resulting in compacts with very low relative density (<80%) that could not form bulk materials with structural integrity or be suitable for performance testing.
